title: Adventure Cycling Association Launches the Eastern Canada Bicycle Route: 930 Miles Linking Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, and Québec City
content:
Adventure Cycling Association‘s newest route, the Eastern Canada Bicycle Route, is 930 miles long, linking Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, and Québec City…

The new Eastern Canada Bicycle Route route runs 65% on bike paths and multi-use trails, offering an approachable international bike tour without a long-haul flight.

Eastern Canada Bicycle Route

Adventure Cycling Association, a leading U.S. bicycle-travel nonprofit, launched the Eastern Canada Route, a 930-mile (1,500 km) bicycle route through southern Ontario and Québec. It connects four of eastern Canada’s most iconic cities: Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, and Québec City. It is Adventure Cycling’s second route, and longest, entirely within the country.

The route runs 65% on bike paths and multi-use trails and is roughly 40% unpaved.

Three research riders physically rode every section in June and July 2026. They checked surface conditions, navigation, safety, and services along the way.

The route is split into three roughly equal sections. Each starts and ends in a major city with air, rail, and bus connections, so riders can tackle the full tour or a single section.

Built on the Trans Canada Trail and La Route Verte

The Eastern Canada Bicycle Route was inspired by two trail networks built by Canadian organizations, communities, and volunteers. The Trans Canada Trail (Sentier Transcanadien) is the world’s longest multi-use trail system, and the route highlights one of its
most popular stretches. La Route Verte, Québec’s provincial cycling network stewarded by Vélo Québec, is one of the longest interconnected cycling networks in North America.

“The Eastern Canada Bicycle Route builds on some of the best cycling infrastructure in North America, created by Canadian communities and organizations like the Trans Canada Trail and Vélo Québec. We utilized the best infrastructure for cycling between Toronto, Ottawa, Montréal, and Québec City, had our research riders test every section, and added detailed navigation and services information. This route is an important part of our growth in serving bicycle travel across North America, and it’s a great eastern counterpart to our Vancouver Crossing Loop and the Canadian section of the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route in the west.” said Jeffrey Mizell, director of routes at Adventure Cycling Association.

Adventure Cycling built on the work of these local organizations, using its 50 years of expertise in creating long distance bike routes to create a specific and unique experience for traveling cyclists. It chose routing suited to loaded touring, added detailed navigation, and documented services, lodging, and riding conditions for every section.

“The Eastern Canada Bicycle Route is an inviting introduction to long-distance bike touring, with manageable terrain, well-spaced services, and an abundance of dedicated bike paths. Whether you’re new to multi-day touring or a seasoned cyclist looking for a rewarding adventure, this route offers an approachable way to experience the landscapes, communities, and culture of eastern Canada,” says Amy Wally, Cartography Program Manager.

Section Highlights

Section 1: Toronto to Ottawa (364 miles / 586 km; 45% bike path, 50% unpaved). Riders leave Canada’s largest city over the Oak Ridges Moraine, then follow crushed-limestone rail trails through Uxbridge, Lindsay, and Peterborough. The route crosses Doube’s
Trestle Bridge and the Ranney Gorge Suspension Bridge, then enters the lakes and forests of the Canadian Shield via remote roads and the K&P Trail. It reaches the national capital through Perth, Smiths Falls, and Carleton Place.

Section 2: Ottawa to Montréal (290 miles / 467 km; 70% bike path, 20% unpaved). The Main Route heads north through Gatineau Valley into the Laurentians through Wakefield and Maniwaki, then routes to Le P’tit Train du Nord, a 145-mile (234 km) former
railway corridor. A more direct River Alternate follows the Ottawa River and Route Verte 1 past Oka National Park.

Section 3: Montréal to Québec City (273 miles / 439 km; 85% bike path, 50% unpaved). From Montréal’s bike network, the route follows the Chambly Canal and La Route Verte through Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Granby, Magog, and Sherbrooke. It then crosses
Québec’s quiet agricultural heartland and finishes with a ferry across the St. Lawrence River into Québec City.

About the Trans Canada Trail

The Trans Canada Trail is the longest multi-use trail system in the world and is always growing. It reaches every province and territory and connects all three of Canada’s coastlines. Each section of the Trans Canada Trail is managed locally and supports different
activities and community needs.

As an organization, the Trans Canada Trail advocates for, stewards, and champions Canada’s nationwide trail system. It is a registered charity that receives funding from the Government of Canada (through Parks Canada), various provincial, territorial, and municipal
governments, and generous donors.

Riders can learn more about the Trans Canada Trail and ways to support it at tctrail.ca and La Route Verte at routeverte.com.

Availability

The Eastern Canada Route is available now as a digital route. Riders navigate with Adventure Cycling’s digital route through Ride with GPS, with riding conditions, services, and points of interest for each section. Visit Adventure Cycling for more.
